common_name: California Dreaming Che (Large-Fruited Upright Mandarin Melon Berry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or rooted-cutting tree in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; California Dreaming is a selection noted for producing larger fruit than most che cultivars along with a more upright growth habit than the sprawling, thorny form typical of seedling che.

directions: Grow like other che selections: full sun and unfussy, well-drained soil, with tolerance for poor, dry, or alkaline conditions that few other fruiting trees can match. California Dreaming is valued among che growers for larger-than-typical fruit and a more upright, tree-like habit that is easier to manage and harvest than sprawling seedling che. As with most che cultivars other than seedless female selections, California Dreaming is generally grown with a male pollinator nearby for reliable fruit set. Fruits ripen in late summer to fall to a maroon-red, bumpy-skinned berry with sweet, melon-like flavor. Young plants can be thorny; formative pruning improves shape and eases harvest.

common_name: Chul Ri Che (Precocious Korean Mandarin Melon Berry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or rooted tree in spring in a range of soil types, keeping roots evenly moist through summer heat; Chul Ri is a Korean che selection notable for bearing a few fruit even in its first year in the ground.

directions: Chul Ri is a fast-growing, precocious female che selection from Korea that can set a light crop in its first year and reaches full production quickly thereafter. Left unpruned it becomes a large multi-stemmed tree, but it responds well to training as a smaller standard; growers commonly graft che onto Osage orange rootstock to encourage tree form over shrubby growth. Requires full sun and consistently moist soil through the heat of summer for best fruit set; like most che other than seedless selections, plant a male pollinator nearby for a reliable crop. Fruits are maroon-red, bumpy-skinned, and sweet with a fig-and-melon flavor.

common_name: Admiral Wilkes Jujube (Historic Late-Season Elongated Jujube)

planting.note: Plant grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Admiral Wilkes is one of the oldest documented jujube introductions to the US, traced to material collected by the US Exploring Expedition in the 1840s and historically grown on the US Capitol grounds.

directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; jujubes are highly drought-tolerant once established and largely untroubled by pests or disease in Gulf Coast conditions. Admiral Wilkes bears elongated, tooth-shaped fruit similar in form to 'Silverhill' but distinguished by very late-season ripening, typically mid-to-late November in most growing regions, useful for extending the jujube harvest well past main-season cultivars like 'Li' and 'Lang'. Fruit skin turns deep reddish-brown at maturity over crisp, juicy, honey-flavored flesh. Historic specimens are noted for exceptional vigor and size.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Teapot (Chinese Chahuzao) is a vigorous, upright Chinese cultivar imported to the US by a university jujube breeding program.

directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; like other jujubes, Teapot is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives on neglect. Its standout trait is fruit shape: medium-sized fruit develop one to five irregular protuberances on the shoulder, most commonly two, giving each fruit a whimsical resemblance to a miniature teapot with a spout and handle, a strong conversation-piece and edible-landscape planting for Gulf Coast gardens. Despite the odd shape, the fruit is very sweet and ripens mid-to-late season, making it a good companion to earlier cultivars like Li or Honey Jar for a longer jujube harvest window. Vigorous, upright tree habit.
sources: New Mexico State University Jujube Breeding Program

common_name: Sweet Lavender Mulberry (Honey-Sweet Lavender-Blushed White Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Sweet Lavender is a self-fertile white mulberry selection valued for very sweet, low-acid fruit that develops random lavender-blushed patches as it fully ripens.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Sweet Lavender is a large, spreading white mulberry that produces heavy, reliable crops of honey-sweet fruit with essentially no detectable acidity or the tannic berry bite found in many mulberries, and the pale fruit blushes lavender in patches when fully ripe. Because the light-colored juice does not stain like black mulberries, it is a good choice for planting near patios and walkways where dropped fruit is a concern. Self-fertile and heat-tolerant once established, with minimal care needed beyond initial establishment watering; fruit ripens over several weeks in early summer and is excellent fresh, dried, or made into jam, juice, or wine.

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in full sun; in zone 9 plant March through June. PKM-2 was developed at an Indian agricultural research institute as an improvement on PKM-1 with heavier lateral branching and much longer pods.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; extremely drought-tolerant once established. PKM-2 is an Indian agricultural selection bred specifically for pod production, producing markedly longer pods than PKM-1 with more flesh relative to seed, and abundant horizontal lateral branching that makes both pods and leaves easier to harvest by hand. It blooms roughly 100-110 days from sowing with first pod harvest around 170-180 days, and leaves have scored well in taste comparisons against other moringa selections. In zone 9, grow as a fast-resprouting tender perennial killed back by frost each winter and regrown from the root or reseeded in spring; commercial growers in India often treat it as an annual, replacing plants after one to two seasons of harvest for peak productivity.

common_name: Bhagya Moringa (KDM-1, Semi-Dwarf Long-Lived Drumstick Tree)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in full sun; in zone 9 plant March through June. Bhagya (also sold as KDM-1) is a semi-dwarf Indian moringa selection developed for smaller stature and long productive life rather than the annual-replant model used for some high-yield selections.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; drought-tolerant once established. Bhagya is a semi-dwarf moringa selection that can be maintained at a manageable height with pruning and training, making it more manageable for home gardens than seedling moringa, which often reaches 20-30 feet. Unlike some high-yield annual selections meant to be replanted every year or two, Bhagya is bred for a long productive lifespan, reportedly remaining in production for many years under good management. It flowers roughly 100-110 days from sowing with first harvest around 160-180 days, producing pods averaging about two feet long. In zone 9, expect frost to kill top growth each winter, with vigorous resprouting from the root base in spring; the compact habit makes it easier to net or protect than larger seedling trees during marginal winters.
